passage:
Thursday, late.

They announced it at 11 today: I'm the new senior associate. My phone lit up all afternoon, and I was happy for about an hour.

Then Nazia walked past my desk without looking up. We've had lunch together nearly every day for two years. She left the office at five sharp with her headphones on, and I felt like I'd done something wrong.

I keep wanting to say sorry. But I worked hard for this, and Nazia knows it. So I didn't apologise and I didn't post anything. I just left a sticky note on her monitor: "Your template saved my first client deck. Thank you. Lunch whenever." 🙂

Maybe the silence is disappointment about her own year, not about me. I'll give it time.

Shreya

qa.q: What did Shreya leave on Nazia's monitor?
qa.a: Shreya left a sticky note thanking Nazia for the template that saved a first client deck and offering lunch whenever Nazia was ready.

qa.q: What does Shreya think might explain Nazia's silence?
qa.a: Shreya thinks the silence may be Nazia's disappointment about Nazia's own year rather than dislike of Shreya, so it is not treated as proof of anger.

qa.q: What did Shreya do well in handling the cold shoulder?
qa.a: Shreya neither apologised for earning the role nor flaunted it; the note credited Nazia's help and left space for the friendship to recover.

qa.q: How might Nazia be feeling as she walks past the desk?
qa.a: Nazia may be feeling the sting of comparison and needing space, so the promotion could feel like a loss for her even though she is fond of Shreya.

grounding: Shreya, newly promoted, senses a friend turning cold and responds by staying warm, crediting the help and allowing time.

passage:
My name is Simran, and I live next door to Maria's parents. I only know what I saw over the wall on Sunday.

Maria's mother had been telling everyone at the temple that Maria was about to be made a manager. That evening Maria arrived, still in her work shoes, and sat down at the table under the veranda light. Her parents stopped talking when she came in.

I couldn't hear all of it, but I heard Maria say, "I didn't get it. Someone else did. I should have told you last week." Her father stared at his tea. Her mother reached over and held Maria's wrist for a moment.

Later the mother came to water the plants, humming. I don't know how she really felt. But Maria was laughing at something by the time I went inside.

qa.q: Where did Simran see Maria sit with her parents?
qa.a: Simran saw Maria sit at the table under the veranda light.

qa.q: What does the mother's touch on Maria's wrist suggest, and how sure can Simran be?
qa.a: Holding Maria's wrist suggests warmth and support, but Simran admits not knowing how the mother really felt, so the inner state is uncertain.

qa.q: What did Maria do that helped with the awkwardness?
qa.a: Maria told her parents plainly that she did not get the role and that she should have said so sooner, instead of letting them hear it from others.

qa.q: How might the parents have felt after telling relatives that Maria was rising?
qa.a: They may have felt awkward or embarrassed in front of the relatives, though their quiet reaction and the later humming suggest they were not blaming Maria.

grounding: Parents had told relatives Maria was rising; a neighbour watches Maria tell them plainly about the setback and the family stay close.

passage:
9:40 pm.

The mind loop is back: I'm not good enough. Meera got the lead role in the account team. I got a polite "next time." So I lay on the sofa scrolling through everyone's promotion posts until my eyes burned.

Then I made myself stop and take a notebook. Evidence of growth: I cut client complaints on my accounts by half this year. I trained two new joiners. I learned the reporting tool nobody wanted to touch. None of that disappears because I lost one seat.

Saurabh texted, "Dinner Saturday?" I said yes. I won't resign in a rage tonight. Tomorrow I'll ask my manager what the gap was, and give it a few months. If nothing changes, I'll look elsewhere with a clear head.

— Sonali

qa.q: What did Sonali list in the notebook?
qa.a: Sonali listed cutting client complaints on the accounts, training two new joiners and learning a reporting tool nobody else wanted.

qa.q: Why did Sonali stop scrolling, and what was Sonali feeling?
qa.a: Sonali was feeling not good enough and stung by comparison, so Sonali stopped scrolling and wrote evidence of growth to separate the loss from self-worth.

qa.q: What could Sonali do next about staying or leaving?
qa.a: Sonali could ask the manager what the gap was and give it a few months, then decide whether to push here or move on.

qa.q: What might Saurabh be offering with the Saturday invitation?
qa.a: Saurabh may be offering company and a break from rumination, showing that Sonali is valued outside any job title.

grounding: Sonali feels 'I am not good enough' after being passed over, separates performance from worth, lists growth evidence, and plans the next step.

passage:
I sit two desks from Ira and across the aisle from Pema, so I saw most of it. Only one team-lead seat was open, and both of them wanted it.

For a week they moved like allies pretending to be neutral. Then I noticed a change. Ira started sending Pema the client's updated file, unasked, with a line like "in case it helps the deck." Pema returned the favour by sharing the pricing sheet. They both worked late, and their slides got much sharper.

Ira didn't win. On the day the email came, Pema walked over to Ira's desk and said, "Your risk slide was better than mine." Ira answered, "Congrats. I'll take the next one."

Maybe they weren't friends. But nobody hid information, and they still eat lunch at the same table. My name is Deepak, by the way.

qa.q: How many team-lead seats were open?
qa.a: Only one team-lead seat was open.

qa.q: What does Ira's sending of the updated client file suggest about Ira's attitude?
qa.a: It suggests Ira wanted to compete by doing strong work, not by hiding information, though the observer cannot be sure of what Ira privately felt.

qa.q: What made this rivalry healthy rather than harmful?
qa.a: Both shared useful files, kept courtesy, and accepted the result without spite, so the competition sharpened their slides instead of breaking trust.

qa.q: How might Deepak, watching from the aisle, see the two rivals?
qa.a: Deepak sees two colleagues who compete but still respect each other; Deepak cannot tell if they are friends, only that no one sabotaged anyone.

grounding: Two colleagues compete for one seat; an observer shows healthy rivalry with shared information and a gracious loss.

passage:
For three years Kunal had been the first to arrive at the Pune office and the last to leave. He believed that if he did excellent work, somebody upstairs would notice. On a Monday in March, the promotion list went up, and it didn't have his name on it. It did have the name of a colleague who attended every leadership lunch.

That evening at a chai stall near the metro station, Kunal told Samir, an older friend from another firm, "I thought loyalty was enough."

Samir stirred his tea. "It's not nothing. But people can only vouch for what they've seen. Who has seen your work?"

Kunal thought about it. Nobody senior had, not really.

The next week he asked to present his supplier project at the monthly review, and he asked his manager to be his sponsor. It felt a little awkward. It also felt real.

qa.q: Where did Kunal talk to Samir?
qa.a: Kunal talked to Samir at a chai stall near the metro station.

qa.q: Why was Kunal so shaken when the promotion list went up?
qa.a: Kunal had believed that loyalty and hard work were enough to be rewarded and that someone upstairs would simply notice.

qa.q: What did Kunal do differently after the conversation?
qa.a: He asked to present his supplier project at the monthly review and asked his manager to sponsor him, so his work became visible to more senior people.

qa.q: How does Samir see the situation differently from Kunal?
qa.a: Samir sees loyalty as valuable but not self-advertising, since people can only support what they have seen, and he guides Kunal without becoming cynical.

grounding: Kunal learns that loyalty and hard work are not automatically rewarded, grieves the belief and learns about visibility and advocacy.

passage:
Okay, so, I'm Nilesh, and the interviewer asked me, "What was the worst part?" Honestly, it wasn't the rumour itself. It was the three weeks of waiting. Somebody in the pantry said, "Cuts are coming to our division," and after that I did the rent maths every night. My EMI, my parents' expectation, my sister's fees. Tarun, my flatmate, found me at the table at 1 am with a calculator.

I could have panicked. I nearly typed an angry post about management. Instead I did the boring things. I moved a little from each salary into a separate account. I updated my resume on a Sunday and quietly messaged two old colleagues. And I kept doing my work well, because I still had it.

Tarun said, "You look like you're planning, not drowning." Some days I was doing both, I'll admit. But planning helped. 🙂

qa.q: What did Nilesh say was the worst part of the layoff rumour?
qa.a: Nilesh said the worst part was the three weeks of waiting after someone in the pantry said cuts were coming.

qa.q: What was Nilesh worried about at the table at 1 am?
qa.a: Nilesh was worried about rent, the EMI, family expectations and a sister's fees, and was doing the maths with a calculator.

qa.q: What did Nilesh do instead of panicking?
qa.a: Nilesh set aside a small buffer each month, updated the resume, quietly messaged two old colleagues and kept doing good work.

qa.q: How does Tarun see Nilesh's state during this time?
qa.a: Tarun sees someone who looks like a planner rather than someone drowning, though Nilesh admits to sometimes doing both at once.

grounding: Nilesh fears rumoured layoffs because of rent, EMIs and family, and responds by building a buffer, updating the resume and continuing to work.

passage:
Monday. Sunaina had given the firm six years. At 10 am, Vikas called her into a room with an HR person and said her role was ending Friday. Two weeks earlier he had promised her a raise "after the restructure." She walked to the stairwell and shook.

Wednesday. The anger hadn't gone anywhere. She typed a furious email to the whole department, read it twice, and saved it in drafts. Then she wrote a different one to HR asking for the terms of her exit in writing, and to Vikas asking, "Would you be willing to give me a reference?" She felt like a fool asking.

Friday. Vikas said yes, and sent a short paragraph about her work that afternoon. She still felt lied to. But she said goodbye to the team, took her contact list, and left with the door unlocked behind her.

qa.q: What did Vikas promise Sunaina two weeks before ending her role?
qa.a: Vikas had promised her a raise after the restructure.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel on Monday, and how do we know?
qa.a: She felt shocked and discarded, shown by her shaking in the stairwell, and she later says she felt lied to.

qa.q: What did Sunaina do with her anger, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She saved the furious email as a draft and asked HR for her exit terms in writing and asked Vikas for a reference, which kept her options and contacts intact.

qa.q: How might Vikas have seen the moment when Sunaina asked for a reference?
qa.a: Vikas may have felt uncomfortable and perhaps guilty, and giving the reference gave him a way to show some respect for her six years.

grounding: After a layoff announced by her boss, Sunaina feels betrayed, gets terms in writing, asks for a reference and keeps bridges intact.

passage:
I still remember how Keerthana began the meeting: "I'm going to be direct, because you deserve that." She told me the division was being cut and my role was included. She didn't hide behind policy words, and she looked at me the whole time.

Then she said she had argued with senior management for a longer notice period and better severance, and won part of it. She offered to write my reference that same afternoon and to introduce me to a contact at a logistics firm.

I was angry with the company and, strangely, grateful to her. My first reflex was to say "You don't have to," but I stopped myself and said, "Thank you. It matters."

We still message every few months. Last week she sent me a job link. I'm Ayesha, and I'll return that kindness one day.

qa.q: What did Keerthana offer Ayesha besides news of the cut?
qa.a: Keerthana offered to write a reference that afternoon and to introduce Ayesha to a contact at a logistics firm, after arguing for better severance.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling towards Keerthana during the meeting?
qa.a: Ayesha was angry with the company but grateful to Keerthana, whose direct and honest manner felt like care.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Ayesha to accept the help and stay in touch?
qa.a: Accepting the reference and thanking Keerthana honoured the effort made for Ayesha, and the connection has already produced a job link.

qa.q: What was it probably like for Keerthana to deliver the news?
qa.a: Keerthana likely found it hard, since she chose to be direct and to fight for severance while carrying out a decision she did not make alone.

grounding: Ayesha is laid off by a manager who is honest, offers a reference and fights for severance; she accepts help and stays in touch.

passage:
Tuesday. The list came out and Noor's name wasn't on it. Thomas's was. Noor sat in the parking lot with her hands on the steering wheel, relieved and sick about being relieved. She texted Thomas, "I'm so sorry." He replied with a thumbs-up and nothing else.

Thursday. Noor stopped saying sorry. She opened her contacts and sent Thomas the names of two hiring managers she knew, plus a note: "Tell them I recommended you." She also asked whether he'd like a written recommendation for his portfolio.

The following Wednesday. Thomas wrote back, "Thank you for not disappearing." They had coffee. Thomas talked about the layoff for a while, and Noor mostly listened. A month later, one of the managers invited him to interview. Noor didn't say anything grand. She just kept the coffee going.

qa.q: How did Thomas first reply to Noor's apology?
qa.a: Thomas replied with a thumbs-up and nothing else.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling in the parking lot?
qa.a: Noor felt relieved to keep her job and sick about being relieved, which shows guilt about surviving when Thomas was laid off.

qa.q: What did Noor do that turned her guilt into help?
qa.a: She shared two hiring managers' names, offered to be a reference and to write a recommendation, and later kept meeting Thomas for coffee.

qa.q: What did Thomas's thank-you suggest about how he had seen Noor's earlier silence?
qa.a: Thomas's thanks for not disappearing suggests he might have feared that laid-off people get avoided, so Noor's steady presence mattered to him.

grounding: A survivor of layoffs feels guilty and turns it into contacts, recommendations and steady presence for a laid-off friend.

passage:
Day one. Kalyani cleared her desk into a cardboard box and sat in her car for a while. Her phone buzzed with messages: "So sorry." "Can I send your resume to my friend?" She felt small, almost embarrassed to read them.

Day three. Ritu, from the next row, texted, "Lunch on me? No talking about jobs unless you want to." They sat at a noodle shop for an hour. Ritu listened, then pulled up a referral form for her old team and said, "I already told them you're good."

Day ten. Kalyani forwarded a referral message to a friend of her own who was also job hunting. She realised it didn't feel like pity. It felt like being part of a place where people looked out for each other.

She wrote to Ritu: "Whenever you need something, I'm here." 🙂

qa.q: Where did Kalyani and Ritu have lunch?
qa.a: Kalyani and Ritu had lunch at a noodle shop.

qa.q: How did Kalyani feel when the messages arrived on the first day?
qa.a: Kalyani felt small and almost embarrassed to read the messages, which shows she found it hard to receive help.

qa.q: How could Kalyani keep the help she receives from feeling like pity?
qa.a: She could accept it with thanks and look for chances to return the favour or pass help on, as she began to do by sharing a referral with a friend.

qa.q: What might Ritu have hoped for when she suggested lunch with no job talk?
qa.a: Ritu may have wanted Kalyani to feel like a friend first, not a case to be fixed, and to choose whether to talk about work.

grounding: Laid-off Kalyani receives messages, referrals and a shared lunch from coworkers, accepts help without feeling small and offers to return it.
